title: Data: A One-Page Scorecard That Spots Trouble Early
summary: How the EOS Scorecard works: five to 15 weekly numbers, one owner each, picked by working backward from results, read as a 13-week trend, and the traps to avoid.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: Data
book.originalTitle: Data: Harness Your Numbers to Go from Uncertain to Unstoppable
book.note: This article is a practical reflection on the book within the EOS context. It is not a substitute for reading the original work.

html:
The monthly business review has a strange rhythm. By the time the P&L shows up, everyone finally agrees on what happened: revenue missed, margin slipped, the support queue doubled. The room now has plenty of evidence and very little time, because the moment when a small fix would have worked was three weeks ago.

The Scorecard chapter of Data is about getting that moment back. The book is the Data Component volume of the EOS Mastery series, written by Mark O'Donnell, Angela Kalemis and Mark Stanley (EOS Worldwide). Its pitch is refreshingly small: most companies don't need more numbers. They need one page of the right ones, read every week, owned by someone who knows what to do when a number turns red.

A Scorecard is a short list with names on it

EOS is specific about what the Scorecard is. You track five to 15 Measurables each week. Each one has exactly one owner and one weekly goal. The leadership team reviews the page in its weekly Level 10 Meeting, and when an off-track number points to a real problem, it goes on the Issues List (EOS Scorecard).

The hard part is deleting. Adding a metric takes ten seconds. Removing one the founder has looked at for years takes a real conversation. If you've ever worked on a monitoring setup where every alert fires, you know how this ends: after two weeks nobody reads the alerts. A Scorecard with forty rows fails the same way.

The numbers you cut don't disappear. They move to department reports or a detailed dashboard you open when something looks odd. The weekly page has a narrower job: show, in a couple of minutes, whether the business is on track and where the team should look first.

A quick test for each row: if this number goes red, does a specific person know which conversation to start? If the answer is "we'd probably talk about it," the number is interesting but it's not ready for the Scorecard yet.

The P&L is the rear-view mirror

The first post in this series compared good numbers to a clean windshield. In that picture, the P&L is the rear-view mirror. You need it, and you can't drive forward by staring at it. Mark O'Donnell puts it plainly: lagging indicators like cash balance, NPS and EBITDA "arrive too late." He'd rather see activities the team can move this week on the Scorecard, such as calls booked or demos held (The <15-Number Rule).

The EOS Scorecard page splits Measurables into two kinds. Activity-based ones are early signals that help predict results. Current-state ones show what needs attention right now. EOS suggests starting with activity-based numbers where you can (EOS Scorecard).

What that looks like by team:

  • Sales: qualified leads, demos booked, proposals sent.
  • Support: overdue tickets, first response time, reopened tickets.
  • Delivery: late orders, orders stuck in the warehouse, cycle time.

Don't get stuck on the labels. The same number can be one team's result and another team's early warning. The useful question is simpler: if this number moves this week, does it tell us something about the next few weeks?

Work backward from the result you want

The most practical way to pick numbers is to start at the result and walk backward. What has to happen right before it? What has to happen before that? Keep going until you reach an activity someone can do and count this week. EOS Implementer Jeremy Hardern describes the same move: take the monthly numbers, which are mostly lagging, and "work backward to define the weekly actions that drive them" (Build a Great Scorecard, Then Make It Better).

Here's a made-up example with round numbers. A small agency wants four new clients a month, roughly one a week. If one in four proposals closes, the team needs four proposals a week. If half of all meetings lead to a proposal, that's eight meetings. If one in ten outreach messages gets a meeting, that's 80 messages. Now the Scorecard has three rows: 80 outreach, 8 meetings, 4 proposals. The revenue goal stopped being a wish. It's a chain of weekly work that everyone can see.

The chain also shows which lever is stuck. Maybe revenue is short because there aren't enough warm leads. Maybe the close rate is fine and the deals are just small. Without the chain, a team can push the wrong lever very hard for a whole quarter.

Weekly beats monthly

O'Donnell's arithmetic is hard to argue with: a monthly rhythm leaves you "only eleven more pivots this year," while a weekly one "offers 51 chances to steer" (same article). Small corrections every week usually hurt less than one sharp turn at the end of the quarter.

EOS also shows 13 weeks of actuals side by side, so the team reads trends instead of reacting to a single week (EOS Scorecard). One red week can be noise. Three weeks of slow slide is worth the agenda.

Weekly doesn't mean jumpy, though. Some numbers need a healthy range more than a direction. Too few leads starves sales. Too many can swamp a small team. For numbers like that, ask where the safe zone is.

And the goals themselves need tuning. O'Donnell suggests a leadership team should hit its weekly goals about 80% of the time. An EOS article makes the other half of the point: if everything is always green, the goals are probably too soft (The EOS Scorecard).

Traps: copied, orphaned and easy metrics

The same EOS article admits that "the first version of a Scorecard is rarely the final version." That's good news. Plenty of teams give up because version one wasn't perfect. Treat the Scorecard like a product: drop a number nobody acts on, add one after a surprise nobody saw coming, raise a goal once the team gets stronger, move a too-detailed number down to a department scorecard.

While you iterate, watch for four traps:

  • Copying another company's Scorecard. Hardern warns it "may introduce blind spots or, worse still, unintended consequences." Their numbers describe their business model.
  • Orphan metrics. O'Donnell lists shared ownership (several names on one number) and red numbers without action among the common pitfalls. Hardern adds a handy rule: if a number keeps missing and nobody seems to care, maybe it doesn't belong on the Scorecard.
  • Using numbers to dodge a people problem. If the leadership team doesn't trust someone in a seat, ten extra metrics won't fix that. It's a People Component conversation.
  • Measuring what's easy. Page views are easier to count than repeat customers, and only one of them tells you whether the business is healthy. It's the old story about searching for your keys under the streetlight because that's where the light is.
What I want to keep

A Scorecard earns its place when it changes what the team does next week. If a number goes red and nobody knows the next step, look at the number before you look at the person who owns it.

Once the leadership Scorecard works, the next post in the series takes numbers down to each person, in a way that helps people do their job instead of feeling watched: Everyone Has a Number.

Try this week

  • List every number shown in your weekly meeting, then cut until five to 15 remain.
  • Write one owner and one weekly goal next to each. A number nobody owns doesn't go on the page.
  • Pick one important result and walk backward to at least one activity you can count every week.
  • Put 13 weeks of data side by side and read the trend, not just last week.
  • For each number, write one line: "If this goes red, the first thing we do is..."

A Scorecard won't run the company for you. It makes the weekly conversation more honest. When everyone looks at the same few numbers every week, the team spends less energy guessing and more on the handful of things that actually move the business.

faqs.a: A one-page weekly report of five to 15 Measurables. Each has one owner and one weekly goal. The leadership team reviews it in its weekly Level 10 Meeting, and an off-track number that signals a real problem goes on the Issues List.

faqs.q: How do you choose Scorecard numbers?
faqs.a: Start from the result you want and work backward to the weekly activities that produce it. EOS suggests favoring activity-based Measurables because they predict results, while lagging numbers like cash balance or EBITDA arrive too late to act on.

faqs.q: Why review numbers weekly instead of monthly?
faqs.a: Mark O'Donnell's math: a monthly rhythm leaves only about 11 more chances this year to change course, while a weekly one gives about 51. EOS also shows 13 weeks side by side so the team sees trends instead of reacting to one odd week.

faqs.q: Can we copy another company's Scorecard?
faqs.a: Use it for ideas, but don't copy it as is. Another company's numbers reflect its business model, stage and constraints, and copying them can create blind spots. Build your own first version, run it weekly and improve it.
